learn.b: An iterable is anything you can loop over, like a list or a string. iter() turns it into an iterator and next() gets the next item. When there are no items left, next() raises StopIteration. A for loop does all of this for you.

it = iter([10, 20])
print(next(it))
print(next(it))

learn.b: A generator function uses yield instead of return. Each yield hands back a value and pauses the function, keeping its variables. The next request resumes right after the yield. Calling the function gives you a generator object, it does not run the body yet.

A generator makes values one at a time only when asked. That means it can describe huge or even infinite sequences without storing them. A generator can be used only once; after it runs out you must create a new one.
learn.code:
def naturals():
    n = 1
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 1

g = naturals()
print(next(g), next(g), next(g))

learn.b: A generator expression looks like a list comprehension but uses parentheses and is lazy. Functions like sum, max and any accept it directly. enumerate() gives index and item pairs and zip() walks several lists together.
learn.code:
print(sum(x * x for x in range(4)))
for i, ch in enumerate('ab'):
    print(i, ch)
print(list(zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b'])))

learn.b: In Python a function is a value. You can store it in a variable, pass it into another function, and return it from a function. A function defined inside another function can use the outer function's variables; this is called a closure.

A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new function that usually wraps the old one. The new function can run code before and after the original. This lets you add features without editing the original function.
Writing @shout above a function is the same as writing hi = shout(hi) after it. The wrapper should accept *args and **kwargs so it works with any function. Return what the original returns.

Wrappers hide the original name and docstring. Put @functools.wraps(func) on the wrapper to keep them. A decorator that takes its own arguments needs one more layer: a function that returns the decorator.

learn.b: A with statement sets something up, runs your block, and always cleans up, even if an error happens. Files, locks and database connections all use it. Without with you must remember to clean up yourself, and mistakes leak resources.

learn.b: Any class with an __enter__ and an __exit__ method works in a with statement. __enter__ runs at the start and its return value goes after as. __exit__ runs at the end, even after an error.

contextlib.contextmanager lets you write a context manager as a generator. Code before yield is the setup and code after yield is the clean up. Use try and finally around the yield so cleanup always runs.

Context managers are good for timing code, changing a setting temporarily, opening files, and locking shared data. If __exit__ returns True it hides the error, so only do that on purpose. You can also stack several in one with line separated by commas.
learn.code:
with open('a.txt') as a, open('b.txt') as b:
    pass

learn.b: Write the contents of containers like list[int], dict[str, int] and tuple[int, str]. A value that may be missing is written str | None. Use these hints to document what your data looks like.
The @dataclass decorator writes __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for you. You list the fields with type hints. It saves lots of boilerplate for classes that mainly hold data.

Fields can have defaults, and defaults must come last. For mutable defaults like lists use field(default_factory=list). frozen=True makes objects unchangeable and order=True lets you compare and sort them.
learn.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Player:
    name: str
    score: int = 0
    tags: list = field(default_factory=list)

p.score += 5
print(p)

learn.b: Recursion means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the problem. Each call gets its own set of variables. Think of Russian dolls: open one and find a smaller one inside.

Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the recursion with a direct answer. The recursive case moves toward the base case, usually by making the input smaller. Without a base case Python raises RecursionError.
Lists and strings fit recursion well: handle the first item, then recurse on the rest. The base case is usually the empty list or empty string. Slicing makes the smaller input.

Python allows about 1000 nested calls by default. Deep recursion can fail, and some recursion repeats work, like a naive Fibonacci. Often a loop is simpler, but recursion is great for trees and nested data.

qs.q: What stops a recursive function?
qs.why: The base case returns without recursing.

qs.q: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?
qs.why: Python stops it with RecursionError.

learn.b: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern for matching text. In Python you use the re module. re.search(pattern, text) finds the first match anywhere and returns a match object or None. Use .group() to get the matched text. Write patterns as raw strings like r'\d+' so backslashes are kept.
learn.code:
import re
m = re.search(r'\d+', 'room 42')
print(m.group())

learn.b: \d is a digit, \w is a letter, digit or underscore, and \s is whitespace. A dot . is any character. + means one or more, * means zero or more, ? means optional, and {3} means exactly 3. ^ is the start and $ is the end of the text. [abc] matches one of the listed letters.
learn.code:
import re
print(re.findall(r'\d{3}', '12 345 6789'))
print(bool(re.match(r'^[a-z]+$', 'abc')))

learn.b: re.findall returns a list of all matches. re.sub(pattern, new, text) replaces matches. re.split splits text at matches. re.match only matches at the very start of the text.
learn.code:
import re
print(re.findall(r'\d+', 'a1b22'))
print(re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', 'a   b    c'))
print(re.split(r',\s*', 'a, b,c'))

learn.b: Parentheses make groups that capture parts of a match. m.group(1) is the first group. Use groups to pull out pieces like a name and a number. Quantifiers are greedy by default and take as much as possible; add ? to make them take as little as possible.
learn.code:
import re
m = re.search(r'(\w+)@(\w+)\.com', 'bo@site.com')
print(m.group(1), m.group(2))

qs.why: \d matches one digit.

qs.why: findall returns every match in a list.

qs.why: \d+ matches runs of digits.

qs.why: Raw strings do not process escape sequences.

learn.b: JSON is a text format for data that almost every language understands. It looks like Python dicts and lists, but keys must be in double quotes and the words are true, false and null. Python converts them to True, False and None.

learn.b: json.loads(text) turns JSON text into Python objects. json.dumps(obj) turns Python objects into JSON text. indent=2 makes it pretty and sort_keys=True orders the keys. The s in the names stands for string.

import json
data = json.loads('{"a": [1, 2]}')
print(data['a'][1])
print(json.dumps({'b': True, 'a': None}, sort_keys=True))

learn.b: json.dump(obj, file) writes JSON to an open file, and json.load(file) reads it back. This is a simple way to save game scores or settings. Always open files with with.
learn.code:
import json
with open('save.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump({'score': 5}, f)
with open('save.json') as f:
    print(json.load(f))

learn.b: A test is code that checks that your code works. When you change something later, tests tell you right away if you broke it. Write small tests with known inputs and expected outputs, and include edge cases like empty input or zero.
assert condition raises AssertionError if the condition is False and does nothing if it is True. You can add a message after a comma. It is a quick way to check your assumptions.
learn.code:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

assert double(4) == 8
assert double(0) == 0, 'zero case'
print('all passed')

learn.b: The unittest module organizes tests in classes that inherit from unittest.TestCase. Each test method name must start with test. Use assertEqual, assertTrue and assertRaises instead of plain assert for clearer messages. unittest.main() runs them all.

Follow arrange, act, assert: set up the input, call the code, check the result. Test one thing per test and give tests clear names. setUp runs before every test to prepare shared data. When a test fails, fix the code, not the test, unless the test is wrong.

qs.why: A failing assert raises AssertionError.

learn.b: A text game keeps its state in variables or a dictionary: where the player is, health, items. The main loop repeats: show the state, read a command, update the state, check for a win or quit. while True with a break is a common way to write it.

Split what the user typed into words with split(). The first word is the verb and the rest are the arguments. A dictionary can map verbs to functions, which is cleaner than a long if chain. Always handle unknown commands politely.
learn.code:
cmd = 'go north'
parts = cmd.split()
verb, arg = parts[0], parts[1]
print(verb, arg)

learn.b: A to-do app is a list of dictionaries, each with text and done. Functions add a task, mark one complete, remove one, and count what is left. Returning values instead of printing makes each function easy to test.
learn.code:
tasks = []
def add_task(tasks, text):
    tasks.append({'text': text, 'done': False})

add_task(tasks, 'milk')
tasks[0]['done'] = True
print(tasks)

learn.b: Keep the logic in small pure functions and keep input() and print() in a thin outer layer. Then you can test the logic with assert and reuse it later in a bigger app. Save data with json when the game or list must remember things.
